comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C71-C74 regarding axon guidance defects. Both evaluations find these neural patterning abnormalities well-supported by immunofluorescence data, though peer reviewers note these may correlate with rather than cause scoliosis.

Perfect agreement on claims C81-C83 regarding EPHA4 and ephrin expression patterns. Both evaluations accept the in situ hybridization and single-cell transcriptome data as supporting the proposed signaling mechanism.

Strong agreement on claims C47-C54 regarding zebrafish scoliosis phenotypes. Both evaluations find the loss-of-function experiments convincing, with quantitative data (88/116 homozygotes affected) strongly supporting EPHA4's role in scoliosis development.

Strong agreement on claims C76-C80 regarding CSF-cN and optogenetic data. Both evaluations accept the neural circuit abnormalities as sound observations, though peer reviewers question the causal link between these defects and scoliosis.

Strong agreement on claims C68-C70 regarding calcium imaging data showing disrupted neural coordination. Both evaluations accept the evidence for CPG dysfunction at the neural activity level as valid.

Agreement on claims C102-C104, which are literature-based citations linking CPG dysfunction to human IS pathophysiology. Both evaluations accept these as appropriate contextual support without challenge.
Agreement on claims C85-C86 regarding efnb3b morphant data. Both evaluations support these findings as phenocopying epha4a mutant defects and validating the ephrin B3-Epha4 signaling pathway.

Agreement on claims C87, C90-C92 regarding NGEF variant identification. Both evaluations accept the genetic data extending EPHA4 pathway findings to related genes, though OpenEval notes lack of functional validation.

Agreement on claims C60-C66 regarding high-speed video analysis of turning behavior. Both evaluations accept the quantitative data on counterbend defects as sound observations, though peer reviewers question causality to scoliosis.

Agreement on claims C55-C59 regarding behavioral analysis and rescue experiments. Both evaluations find the data sound, with appropriate quantification and statistical testing validating EPHA4's role.

Partial overlap on claims C24-C30, C32 (functional characterization of variants). Both evaluations support the genetic evidence, with peer reviewers explicitly stating human genetic data are 'quite convincing.' OpenEval also covers these claims while peer review R1 includes broader genetic findings.

Partial overlap on claims C16, C22 regarding EPHA4 identification. Both evaluations support the genetic finding, though OpenEval notes the marginal p-value (0.045) warrants caution while peer reviewers find the overall genetic data 'quite convincing.'
Partial overlap on claims C33-C36 regarding WGS and splicing defect validation. Both evaluations support these findings as part of the convincing human genetic evidence linking EPHA4 variants to IS.

Partial overlap on claims C37-C41 regarding PAX3 deletion case. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to 36-gene deletion making attribution speculative, while peer reviewers include this in their overall acceptance of 'quite convincing' human genetic data.

Partial overlap on claims C42-C45 regarding GWAS and eQTL data. Both evaluations support this convergent evidence, with OpenEval noting modest common variant p-value (0.023) while peer reviewers accept it as part of convincing genetic evidence.

Key disagreement on claims C100-C101 regarding CPG dysfunction causing scoliosis. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN noting the causal link is not experimentally demonstrated. Peer reviewers similarly state this conclusion 'is not fully supported' and that impaired movements may 'simply coincide with, but do not cause' scoliosis.

Disagreement on main conclusions C93, C112. OpenEval finds these well-supported by convergent evidence, while peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, stating the CPG-to-scoliosis causal model 'is a reasonable idea, but currently not strongly backed up by data.'

Disagreement on mechanistic model claims C106-C107, C110. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN noting the specific steps are speculative and not directly demonstrated. Peer reviewers similarly find the model not fully supported, requiring 'independent methods of disrupting CPG function' to validate causality.

OpenEval evaluates background claims C1-C13 as supported by published literature. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as reviewers focused on primary findings rather than background context.
OpenEval evaluates claim C31 (EPHA4 function context from Fu et al., 2007) as supported established knowledge. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
OpenEval evaluates claims C94-C96 (literature context on novelty) as supported. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as these are contextual citations rather than primary findings.
OpenEval evaluates claims C97-C99 (literature context for zebrafish findings) as supported. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
OpenEval evaluates claims C108-C109 (companion study validation) as supported by citation to Wang et al., 2024. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

Peer reviewers evaluate claims C17, C19, C105 as part of their UNCERTAIN assessment of the CPG-to-scoliosis causal model. OpenEval addresses C105 in R21 (SUPPORTED) and C17, C19 are not explicitly evaluated separately by OpenEval.
